@@8512058 <h> Canada needs an ' Own the Podium ' strategy for clean energy <h> Canada 's clean tech sector is poised to compete , but it will take more than a healthy startup environment , where venture capital and a bit of luck can make a winner . <p> Photograph courtesy of Wikimedia Commons , by J ? rgen <p> By TOM RAND <p> PUBLISHED : Wednesday , April 27 , 2016 1:47 PM <p> Last week 's signing of the Paris climate accord marks the start of a new age , with huge implications for Canada . The fossil fuels that power the global economy today are entering a permanent -- if slow -- decline . Gone are cozy assumptions of endless growth in oil exports . Winners in the high stakes global energy market of the 21st century are those countries that can scale up exports of cutting edge clean energy technology . Canada 's clean tech sector is poised to compete , but it wo n't win without support . We need an ' Own the Podium ' strategy for clean energy . <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ market is worth more than $300 billion annually , and is estimated to grow to a trillion dollars by 2020 . Other countries that see the sector 's potential are beating us to the punch . Canada had a decent head start , but is losing ground fast . Between 2008 and 2015 , our market share dropped by nearly three-quarters . That adds up to more than a hundred billion dollars of lost business . <p> We can get that market share back , but it will take more than a healthy startup environment , where venture capital and a bit of luck can make a winner . Clean tech ventures are nothing like web startups . Entrepreneurs ca n't disrupt the energy industry with a clever new app . Think Bombardier , not Uber . It takes a lot of time and capital to build a company capable of competing in global energy markets . Winners need to sell utility-scale equipment that can beat fossil fuels at its own game . <p> Backing loans gives banks confidence <p> Clean energy projects , like traditional infrastructure , are highly capital @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's a solar farm in Africa , energy storage system in California or biofuel factory in China , developers borrow money to build energy systems . It 's bankers who provide the debt that approve technology choices . That 's a problem for innovators because bankers are allergic to technical risk ; they love old stuff , not new . The trick to selling cutting-edge technology is to give those bankers comfort the debt will be paid back . In other words , back the loans . <p> That 's precisely what Export Development Canada ( EDC ) has been doing successfully for decades with established companies exporting into traditional markets . They 've long provided a backstop so Canadian companies ' customers can borrow the money they need to make the purchase . But EDC is not set up to support new sectors like clean tech . They ca n't play ball if the Canadian seller does n't have a large balance sheet . In other words , EDC helps old , established industries -- not new ones . <p> That 's where creative public policy comes in . Targeted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by providing support for first commercial projects in global markets . A loan guarantee , or other incentives to lower the barrier to traditional capital , can get companies through this ' valley of death . ' That means not just picking winners , but backing them ; an ' own the podium ' approach for our proven up-and-comers . It 's a catalyzing role , not permanent support . By the time the company wins the second , or third contract then EDC and the private sector can step in to play their traditional role . <p> Protecting the Canadian job market <p> Canada has precious few potential global champions with proven technology , big markets and the capacity to disrupt global energy flows . It 's taken a decade of patient public and private capital to build them . Without targeted support they will undoubtedly get snapped up by innovation-hungry Chinese conglomerates or cash-rich global corporations , who are already sniffing around . Other countries will lower their emissions using technology we developed . Which is great for the planet , but lousy for the Canadian job market and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The collapse of the oil and gas industry has already cost Canada a lot of jobs . Scores of coal companies across North America have gone belly up . Alberta 's high carbon bitumen will remain at risk . We need to find new and growing export opportunities . In a world starting to grapple with climate change , clean energy technology is a good bet . Canada has maybe a dozen clean energy champions on the verge of global success . To win in this market we need to get behind those winners . And own the clean energy podium .

@@8522732 <h> Rather than a patchwork of provincial policies , a Canada-wide system would send a stronger signal that a low-carbon future is upon us <p> Environment Minister Catherine McKenna should pursue a Canada-wide cap-and-trade system , which would achieve the best outcomes for the environment and the economy , while respecting each province 's autonomy , writes Jamison Steeve . <p> By:Jamison Steeve Published on Thu Apr 28 2016 <p> Over the last decade , in the absence of federal leadership , Canadian provinces have gone their own way on carbon pricing . Alberta chose a unique carbon pricing system , British Columbia implemented a carbon tax , and Quebec launched a cap-and-trade system which Ontario will soon join . Others are waiting in the wings , either weighing their options or vehemently opposed . As a result , Canada 's environmental standing fell and full economic potential went untapped . <p> Now that the country has an engaged federal government that is determined to act on climate change , things are likely to take a new direction . Provinces that are n't pursuing any form of carbon @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ current musing is that the federal government will set a $15 carbon tax to act as a minimum carbon price . But is a national price floor enough , or should the federal government consider other options ? The problem is that $15 is not enough to drive the deep emissions reductions needed . Without a hard cap , population and economic growth will drive growth in emissions . Furthermore , it is hard for governments to commit to continually increasing a tax ; whereas it is not too difficult to continually tighten the cap in accordance with emissions targets . <p> Cap-and-trade is the best way for Canada to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions and still maintain economic growth and competitiveness . Rather than having multiple provincial auctions , the administrative costs of the program would be minimized through co-ordinated joint auctions across provinces . The system would operate similarity to the Western Climate Initiative 's system , where each province puts up a number of allowances for auction , and all provinces bid on the common pool of allowances . A countrywide carbon price would be determined . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Canada 's commitment to reducing emissions to 80 per cent below 1990 levels by 2050 . Auction revenue would be distributed across the provinces , in line with their respective allocation of emissions ( determined using 1990 levels ) . This way , each province contributes evenly to achieving Canada 's goal . Doing so will ensure that Canada is able to fulfil its international commitment while ensuring fairness across provinces . <p> Rather than a patchwork of provincial policies , a Canada-wide system would send a stronger signal to businesses and investors that a low-carbon future is upon us . This will help businesses make better informed investment decisions . <p> If Canada as a whole puts a hard cap on emissions , the domestic demand for low-carbon ( clean-tech ) goods and services will increase . This will help the country develop its clean-tech market , providing space to grow and sell to a domestic market , eventually maturing , exporting and capturing global market share . <p> With a common carbon price across provinces , interprovincial competitiveness concerns related to asymmetric climate policy are alleviated -- firms can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ borders . This reduces the carbon leakage that more environmentally progressive provinces would face under asymmetric climate policy . <p> Another major benefit to a common Canadian market is that , when engaged in allowance trading across provinces , each province benefits . In our most recent paper , we find that Ontario 's economic outcomes are improved when firms are able to import cheaper allowances from low-cost regions , like California . Under a pan-Canadian system , through allowance trading , high-cost provinces would benefit from lower compliance costs , while firms in low-cost provinces would increase their profits by abating and selling excess allowances . <p> A Canada-wide cap-and-trade system would achieve the best outcomes for the environment and the economy , while respecting each province 's autonomy . Provinces would be allowed to use auction revenues as they see fit -- whether to invest in low-carbon technology , infrastructure , cut other taxes , issue household transfers , etc . Each region also has the autonomy to issue free allowances to at-risk industries in order to minimize the costs on businesses and address competitiveness concerns . This should @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ resource-dependent provinces , like Alberta and Saskatchewan . <p> To be frank , a $15 price floor does almost nothing to guarantee that the country lives up to its international commitments . A national cap , on the other hand , with obligations spread evenly across provinces , will allow the country to address climate change while providing best outcomes for the economy . <p> It feels as though Canada may be on the cusp of fulfilling its role in fighting climate change , while still ensuring the economic growth we need . There is a model wherein we can have both federal leadership and provincial control . The prime minister and the premiers can have a thoughtful conversation about carbon pricing and pipelines at the same time . Now is the time to do so together , rather than at odds with one another , and take our place on the global stage as both an economic and environmental leader . <p> Jamison Steeve is executive director of the Institute for Competitiveness &amp;amp ; Prosperity . The Institute published a working paper this week : " Toward a low-carbon economy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @

The numerous trade associations , think tanks , lobbyists and others receiving money from our companies ' treasuries is unknown . <p> That 's changing and smarter companies are getting ahead of the curve . This year our institutional investor clients filed the first Canadian shareholder proposals on political spending disclosure at Enbridge Inc. and TransCanada Corp . and we engaged in productive discussions with both companies on their behalf . As a result , both have set a new bar by agreeing to disclose new information on how and where they spend on political activity , as well as establishing new board-level oversight for that spending . Shareholders will vote on a similar proposal at Suncor at its upcoming annual meeting and we expect to see additional disclosure from that company as well . <p> Canadian citizens need a strong regulatory regime around corporate political contributions and it 's up to politicians to strengthen those rules . The question speaks to all facets of governing : partisan politics , administration , decisions flowing from the judiciary , the never-ending calls for greater transparency and accountability requirements , and the thinking that management in the public sector can be made to look like the private sector . And , unlike the private sector , government is expected to pursue activities whether or not it is good at delivering them . <p> It is government that is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ignore a national disaster , be indifferent to an aboriginal community facing a political or economic crisis , or avoid raging debate about the impact of climate change . Wicked problems have no visible beginning or end . They require investing resources with no assurance that the desired benefits will be achieved and often without the tools to assess the impact . If government decides to avoid dealing with society 's wicked problems , they will be left unattended . The cost to society over the longer term would be prohibitive . <p> All government activities are tied to Parliament , to partisan politics and the incessant demands of the 24-hour news cycle . This requires politicians to be good at generating blame , avoiding blame , playing to a segment of the population to win the next election and avoiding risks . And it requires senior public servants to be good at embracing and defending the status quo , adding management layers and staff , keeping ministers out of trouble in the news media , responding to the demands from the prime minister and his office , and managing a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> It is important to stress that the prime minister , ministers , and many senior public servants see considerable merit in the ability of government to be good on all these points . It comes with the territory and it is their territory . They set the rules . It is the most important measure of success , and for them government has to be good at these things if it is to be good at anything else . <p> Conversely , government is not as good as it once was at implementing policy , managing human and financial resources with efficiency and frugality , innovating and dealing with non-performers , paying sufficient attention to service delivery and front-line workers , and evaluating the impact of policies and programs . <p> Over the years , we have added one program after another , one unit after another to the machinery , one officer of Parliament after another , while expanding central agencies and making them responsible for a wide variety of activities . Taken in isolation , one may be able to justify each new program , new unit @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are taken together , we have created a machinery that can no longer operate efficiently as it tries to deliver programs and services in an era of permanent election campaigns . <p> Being good at managing the blame game matters a great deal in the Ottawa bubble and in the national media , but less so elsewhere . Adding oversight bodies and rules and regulations has made the federal public service not only thicker but also more Ottawa-centric . Other than opposition politicians calling for still more oversight , no one is happy with the incessant calls for more rules and regulations . Morale in the federal public service has plummeted and surveys reveal that citizens are unhappy with the quality of public service . <p> One can only applaud the Clerk of the Privy Council 's recent call for public service to be better at taking risks , delivering front-line services , and producing change and making it stick . @@8529379 <h> Comment : A day in the life of a Syrian refugee-camp volunteer <p> LESBOS , GREECE -- The refugee tsunami flowing onto Greek shores is the first wave of climate-change human migrations likely to occur as a result of increasing global-warming weather events . Syria experienced an acute 10-year dry spell , bankrupting farmers and contributing to ethnic tensions and civil war . <p> Canadians should learn how to respond , because climate change is happening and parts of this planet will be evacuated . Otherwise , we may elect a Donald Trump to keep refugees out by building walls . <p> Greek volunteers make food for refugees inside Moria , a Greek refugee camp for about 3,000 people on the island of Lesbos . And international volunteers , like my family from Vancouver Island , come to help them . <p> Our Greek friends start cooking in an open area with many hungry families and bored young men -- no crowd control except shouting , under a hot sun with no shade . I decide , nervously , to organize the men 's food line , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ I place my 69-year-old body between the two seething sweaty conga-lines converging at the food table , raising my clasped hands in , I hope , the calming position of a Buddhist monk . <p> Hey , these young men are full of testosterone , many experiencing huge personal loss and suffering , only to find themselves cooped up with nothing to do . Under these circumstances , I , too , would be rowdy . <p> I am surrounded by yelling and a multitude of strange , swirling faces , from Somalian to Syrian . For several hours , I sway and sweat between the two wavy lines , maybe exerting a calming effect . Maybe . <p> Where are those PhDs in human-migration policy ? Where are the trauma counsellors ? <p> I admit to being angry immediately after this exhausting exposure to chaos . But my wife , Margaret , and I talk our way to composure , taking deep breaths in the meagre shade of the prison wall . <p> On leaving , I see workers whitewashing that same wall . Just the right soothing metaphor , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for the Pope on his arrival the next day . <p> The shores of Lesbos -- much smaller than Vancouver Island -- received an unbelievable half-million refugees this past year . Wrecked rubber boats litter its beaches . My son , Roan , uses his strong body to cut them up and carry them to disposal areas . <p> In my village of Scala Sikamenaes , a Greek fisherman named Stratis Valiamosis humbly rides by us on a bicycle . He has been nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize for saving dozens of refugees from drowning . How great is that ? <p> Governments , including Canada , are failing to look after these refugees adequately . But international volunteers are answering the call . It 's an unprecedented , citizen-led , humanitarian response to a crisis caused , in part , by climate change .

@@8535127 <h> The Universe from your own back yard - The sunny side of climate change <p> After last week 's article where I suggested you stand around in the dark trying to see Jupiter 's moons through binoculars ( admittedly a challenge ) , the signing of the Paris climate change agreement last Friday has prompted me to recommend an activity that requires no binoculars , or effort , at all . <p> Find a sunny spot sheltered from the cool spring winds , and stand in it . Nice , huh ? <p> The Sun is essentially a large ball of hydrogen and helium involved in a runaway nuclear reaction , and it 's close enough to annually give millions of us radiation burns , although most prefer to call it a ' tan ' . It is simultaneously harmful and benevolent . It is the source of virtually all heat on the surface of the Earth ( volcanism heats the interior ) , and responsible for virtually 100% of our weather , and , over time , climate . <p> The Sun varies between low and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ although it 's been a little erratic recently . It is this solar cycle that drives our weather . The best indicator of the intensity of solar activity is the number of sunspots , areas of intense magnetic storms on the Sun 's surface . The higher the solar activity , the more sunspots you see . We are currently coming off a high period , but one which was lower than average . No reason ; it just was . This follows a longer than normal minimum around 2009 , where solar activity appeared to take a few years off before picking up again . <p> This unusual solar cycle means is that the normal heating and cooling cycles we 've grown to expect on Earth have been a little random these last few years , making the weather a little had to predict . So , why the weather is a bit weird is easy to explain ; the Sun 's acting strange . Why the Sun 's acting strangely is not known , but records back over the centuries have recorded that this is nothing new . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ done lots of odd things in the past , and will undoubtedly do unusual things in the future . It 's a star ; that 's what stars do . What can we do about it ? ' Absolutely nothing ' , and that 's what politicians around the world have just agreed to do over the next few decades with billions of your tax dollars . <p> In Douglas Adams ' sci-fi novel ' The Hitchhiker 's Guide to the Galaxy ' , it turns out that ( spoiler alert ) the answer to The Ultimate Question of Life , the Universe and Everything , is 42 . Fans of Adams ' books know he writes humorous fiction . What is n't funny is that too many people do n't realize that the manmade climate change crowd is feeding them science fiction as well . <p> Climate change is real , but as usual , facts are optional when politics is involved . The fact is , you and I have an almost negligible impact on the world 's climate . The science of astronomy points to the real culprit @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sheltered spot , in your own back yard . <h> Comments <h> NOTE : To post a comment you must have an account with at least one of the following services : Disqus , Facebook , Twitter , Google+ You may then login using your account credentials for that service . @@8551453 <p> LOS ANGELES-- ( Business Wire ) --A Los Angeles-based solar developer will build the largest solar Feed-in Tariff project in the nation this year , a 2 million-square-foot rooftop solar array that will power Los Angeles homes with clean energy while generating hundreds of jobs in low-income neighborhoods near the Port of Los Angeles . <p> The project on the roofs of the Westmont Drive buildings will generate 16.4 megawatts of solar energy for Los Angeles Department of Water and Power ( LADWP ) customers , more than triple the capacity of the next largest Feed-in Tariff project , located in East Los Angeles . <p> The Westmont project will produce enough clean energy to power 5,000 Los Angeles homes , and in the process eliminate carbon emissions equivalent to taking 6,000 cars off the streets . Over the life of the 20-year lease , it 's estimated the project will generate $76 million in revenue from clean energy sold back to LADWP , with 85 to 90 percent of revenues going back to the building owner . The project will create 500 new local jobs . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at the 10th anniversary of the Los Angeles Business Council 's Sustainability Summit , where hundreds of leaders from across the public and private sectors gathered to discuss the most pressing sustainability issues of our day , including solar power , sustainable water and energy and climate change . <p> The Westmont project is the latest , and largest , project to take advantage of LADWP 's Feed-in Tariff ( FiT ) program , which enables building owners to turn their rooftops into solar power plants and sell the power they generate for distribution on the City 's power grid . @@8551465 <p> The prime minister 's first six months have been a whirlwind of activity . There will be no let-up in the next year . We should hope that the opposition parties -- both leaderless and occasionally listless -- can find a way to hold the government to greater account . <p> Justin Trudeau 's government is an activist one . This is partly image , to be certain . He has undertaken an incredible charm offensive both at home and abroad . Polling numbers -- at least at the top line -- suggest that it has worked . His approval ratings remain sky-high , and while his ministers have made some mistakes , the opposition has not been successful in sustaining any prolonged critiques . Trudeau is not the only one wearing a Teflon suit . <p> But it is not all image . The government has been busy . Its budget has substantially undone some of the key tax policies of the last government . It has appointed senators under its new model of appointment , including estimable Peter Harder , who now acts as the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on assisted dying , signed a far-reaching climate change accord , withdrawn fighter jets from Syria and Iraq and replaced them with soldiers , and has begun the process of reforming the electoral system . This government has earned its favourable coverage . <p> But if the government has been busy , it still has much work to do . The aforementioned bill on assisted dying needs to be in place within months . Approval for the Trans-Pacific Partnership remains . Our entire electoral system is to be changed within a year . And what of missing and murdered indigenous women ? And how will all of this be shepherded through a mid-reform Senate ? <p> This is the challenge of the government , but it is also the challenge of the opposition parties . Their task is to figure out how to effectively hold to account a government that has gotten the better of them for the last six months . The more activist this government is , the more important is this task . <p> We can think about government accountability in at least two ways . First , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . This is one of the functions of Parliament : to force the government to explain its legislation and to allow members of both houses to scrutinize that legislation , make recommendations and eventually vote for or against the legislation . Second , there is the accountability that occurs at an election , when ( some ) voters pass judgment on the record of the government over the last four years . <p> How well voters carry out this second function at the next election remains to be seen . First , a long line of research suggests that voters are myopic , and that they are largely unable to objectively assess the records of governments . Second , our next election may well occur under a system that makes electoral sanction more , not less , difficult . <p> What should concern us now is how well Parliament can carry out its first function . Already , some facts appear clear . First , this government will be operating at a torrid pace and on multiple fronts . It will not be simple to maintain sustained critiques . It wo @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a focus on the leader rather than his legislation . Second , like virtually every government before it , this one is willing to provide a favourable accounting of its actions . The first example is the budget . No less an authority than the former parliamentary budgetary officer has suggested that it continues substantial obfuscation . Second , the government 's focus on " deliverology " is a largely desirable one . Governments should have targets and they should attempt to meet them . But those targets are political choices , not objective ones . Another job of the opposition will be not only to keep the government accountable to those targets , but to argue why those targets are insufficient , or wrongheaded . <p> The opposition faces a task as difficult as the prime minister 's . We should wish them luck . <p> Peter Loewen is an associate professor in the department of political science and the Munk School of Global Affairs at the University of Toronto . <h> Comments <p> We encourage all readers to share their views on our articles and blog posts . And , if it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ capital of the world because of its Wild West stock exchange , peopled with colourful touts like Murray Pezim . <p> Before Expo , alcohol could only be sold on Sundays with a restaurant meal . It gave rise to what I hope is an apocryphal story about the restaurant that kept reselling a single cheese sandwich . Today , there 's a pot shop on every corner and a thriving craft beer industry . <p> The self-described " cr ? me-de-la-cr ? me " lived on the west side ; immigrants and the working class lived east of Main . As for the suburbs ? Boundary Road was aptly named because some Vancouverites sniffily proclaimed that they 'd only cross it if they were going to Hope or beyond . Newcomers like me were told often enough that it 's too bad no one had pulled up the drawbridge to Vancouver long ago . Sound familiar ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's glib to credit or blame Expo 86 for all the change . The whole world was changing and Vancouver , British Columbia and Canada were swept along . <p> Canada had only repatriated its constitution and passed the Charter of Rights and Freedoms four years earlier . In the decades that followed , most of the changes were as dramatic as they were unpredicted . The Soviet Union fell . China rose . Globalization . Urbanization . Trade liberalization . Climate change . Disruptive technologies . Terrorism . <p> In early 1980s , resource-dependent Vancouver and British Columbia were hard hit by the worldwide recession . Exports had tanked . Unemployment rates were double-digit . Interest rates soared to 20 per cent . Housing prices fell so far that many were worth less than their mortgages . <p> Unsurprisingly , the billion-dollar Expo party was controversial -- even more so than the 2010 Winter Olympics . Place Stadium , the first convention centre , and the Coquihalla Highway . The Ontario pavilion morphed into Science World . <p> The ruling party -- Social Credit -- was re-elected only 10 days after the fair closed . But Expo ( or at least the sale of the False Creek site ) also defeated it and destroyed the party . <p> For Vancouver , the critical change occurred before Expo . The 1985 agreement set out the terms for the return of Macau and Hong Kong to Chinese control in 1997 when Britain 's 99-year leases expired . It set off years of controlled panic that Canadian politicians believed could be leveraged to economic advantage . <p> Canadian immigration policies were amended to favour well-educated , economic migrants . They included a poorly conceived investor immigrant program . <p> That program gave away permanent residency to anyone with a net value of $1.6 million who was willing give the government an interest-free loan of $800,000 . That has led to calls for another substantial immigration policy overhaul . <p> Expo was the catalyst that brought visibility and cash to Vancouver , which in turn has made it vibrant , more interesting , more diverse and , yes , more livable . <p> It 's now so frequently on the lists of best cities that when a new one comes out it barely rates a mention . <p> But , of course , there 's been a down side . @@8562234 <h> Fast trains loom large for future <h> Fast trains loom large for future <p> China Railways high speed trains at the Beijing South Railway Station . <p> Intercontinental air travel is projected to grow faster than the supply of pilots . But the future of regional travel belongs not to the air but to high-speed trains . This has implications for economic growth . The world 's four top economies are dealing with this differently . <p> Fans of Murder on the Orient Express or The Great Railway Bazaar will have some idea of how trains once stitched Europe together . In two days , one could cross the continent , ensconced in sleeping car and classy restaurant . And one still can in the U.S. , more or less . The pace of these old trains was -- and still is -- leisurely . Yet , for 100 years or so , they were a revolutionary technology that built much of the western world 's economy . Now Japan , Europe and China are building lots of high-speed rail . North America 's a different story @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mass-transit high-speed train , the Shinkansen , initially linking Tokyo and Osaka . Extended to 3,000 kilometres of special track and running up to 320 km/h , the Shinkansen train system is nearly mature . It showed high-speed rail is safe , has least cost per person mile and helps the whole economy . <p> In the 1980s , France followed with the TGV . Today , high-speed technologies and concerns about climate change are driving a new rail revolution throughout western Europe . Smooth welded rails snake up river valleys and through mountain passes to link major cities . For example , ? BB 's Railjet trains link Austria with Switzerland , Hungary , Germany and the Czech Republic at speeds that routinely top 230 km/h . Thus , leaving every two hours , a relaxing train can whisk you from Vienna to Munich with Wi-Fi and good food , in four hours city centre to city centre ; you can show up just before departure and you never wait in line . If you must change trains , some " legal " connections are as short as a few @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and pay more to fly . Europe 's investment in high-speed rail , already tens of billions , could be central to its economic rebirth . Already , building infrastructure is supporting the economy . <p> Six time zones away , much is changing in China . With the world 's worst pollution , it leads the world in green technologies and infrastructure . Around Chinese New Year , the China Rail Corporation moves 150 million passengers . China has 20,000 km of high-speed rail in operation , more than half the world 's total and soon to be three-quarters . And for China , too , building the new rail system is contributing to economic growth that has tripled that of the U.S. <p> North American rail travel has been the poor cousin . In the U.S. , Amtrak has trouble keeping slow trains on its rails . Its Acela Express is America 's only operating high-speed train . The Acela covers 700 km between Washington , D.C. and Boston at speeds up to 240 km/h . But the track is shared , it uses old infrastructure and average speed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ take this train outnumber those who fly . More may be on the way : the California High-Speed Rail Authority is building track between Los Angeles and San Francisco . <p> Other projects are mooted in the U.S. , but not underway . Of these , one stands out because it uses new technology . Elon Musk 's proposed Hyperloop would propel passenger pods on air bearings through an elevated tube in near-vacuum at up to 800 km/h . Its projected cost is less than that of ( ' obsolete ' , Musk calls it ) high-speed rail . Companies are vying to be first to build its twin tubes on pylons next to freeways . Think downtown LAX to SFO in maybe 30 minutes . If it works , it will change the high-speed transport game . <p> Canada , where high-speed rail may be more popular than motherhood , is the only G7 country that has none , though Bombardier is a world leader in building it . The federal government is ramping up infrastructure spending , but proposals for high-speed track in eastern and western corridors or linking @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ building soon . By the time Canada gets high-speed , Europe may be tearing up its track . Perhaps we , too , should take a long look at Musk 's concept . <p> Colin Gillespie is a physicist and author whose most recent book is Time One : Discover How the Universe Began . He writes a weekly web blog Science Seen . <p> You can comment on most stories on winnipegfreepress.com . You can also agree or disagree with other comments . All you need to do is be a Winnipeg Free Press print or e-edition subscriber to join the conversation and give your feedback . 
@@8562279 <h> Eco-Marxism a flawed world view <p> What Lenin , Trotsky and Stalin tried to bring through the front door , Naomi Klein , Avi Lewis and David Suzuki are trying to sneak through the back . The noted wordsmith Conrad Black found exactly the right term to describe the Leap Manifesto : Eco-Marxism . <p> The Leap Manifesto is simply an attempt to reintroduce Marxist principles , ones comprehensively rejected across the globe during the 20th century , by wrapping them in the cloak of environmental exigency : global climate change . <p> There is no doubt the climate is changing ( it always does ) , the pace of change is rapid and largely human induced . It poses a serious challenge . But is a return to Marxism the solution ? Certainly not . <p> Had the authors of the Leap Manifesto not wanted to draw attention to its Marxist origins they would have changed the name . So let us look at the record of Marxism 1.0 in addressing environmental problems . It is n't pretty . <p> Stalin preferred heavy industry to a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the Soviet Union were treated as open sewers : even today half of Russia 's surface water remains fouled with chemical and human waste . Air quality in Soviet cities was the worst in the world . The U.S.S.R. dumped reactors and spent nuclear fuel into the sea and drained one of the largest lakes in the world , the Aral Sea , for irrigation . <p> What did Marxism 1.0 do for climate change ? Here the record is considerably better . Greenhouse gas production in Russia plummeted with the implosion of the post-Soviet economy in the 1990s . Therein lies the secret to how the Leap Manifesto could abate climate change : by fostering widespread economic collapse . <p> The Leap Manifesto presents a utopian vision of future society , one liberated from the evils of capitalism and the oppression of global trade . By insisting on local production , we will recapture manufacturing jobs lost overseas . Instead of importing bananas grown in warm climates , we will live on locally grown produce ( more kale ) in rural agrarian societies . But with bullet trains . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is that since petroleum-based fertilizer is verboten , we will need a couple of extra planets for the land required by low-intensity agriculture to feed the global population . However , I do look forward to catching a fast train to Tuktoyaktuk . <p> Instead of the inherent waste associated with corporations providing citizens with what they want , central planning will choose what we need . This , obviously , is much more efficient . <p> We do n't need , for example , modern automobiles that capitalism has wastefully presented in a dizzying array of choices , from the utilitarian Honda Civic and Ford F-150 to the technologically advanced Toyota Prius and Tesla Model 3 . These will be replaced with people-carriers . Who can forget the Soviet bloc marquee brands such as the Trabant , Yugo , Wartburg and Lada ? <p> For decades , the Trabant was the only car choice for East Germans . With a body built from cotton and wood waste soaked in resin , it was powered by a two-stroke engine that belched thick , black smoke . Brake lights and turn signals @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ buy them . Wait times for delivery averaged 11 to 15 years . <p> Though lacking panache , these vehicles contained elements of innovation . Soviet engineers thoughtfully provided rear-window defrosters on Yugos so the people pushing them could warm their hands . <p> It promised to create jobs in the green economy , and it has . But for every new job created , two to four jobs were lost elsewhere because of spiralling electricity costs , fuelled by wildly inflated purchase prices for wind and solar energy . This energy is produced at times and seasons out of phase with demand , resulting in surplus production that must be sold at a heavy loss . The prime beneficiary of Ontario 's green-energy policy has been the American consumer who gets power subsidized by the Ontario ratepayer . <p> And while the McGuinty-Wynne fiasco was unfolding , the private-sector ( capitalism ) quietly delivered renewable energy at or below grid cost for Americans from California to New York . <p> Government , on behalf of the people , can guide the change we want . Renewable energy is part of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ providing temporary incentives . The McGuinty-Wynne solution in its Leap involved less twig-bending and more the planting of entire tree farms . <p> Why the Leap Manifesto and Marxism 2.0 are doomed from the outset is why Marxism 1.0 failed . As John Stuart Mill long ago observed , socialists underestimate the natural indolence of humans . Capitalism provides the necessary incentive system for people to work harder and innovate more . Greed , within limits , is good . <p> It was the lifelong Marxist , Christopher Hitchens , who diagnosed Marx 's great failing : Marx , he observed , " ultimately failed to grasp quite how revolutionary capitalist innovation was . " <p> It is capitalist innovation that brought us the Honda Civic , Toyota Prius and Tesla Model 3 , not Trabants and Yugos . <p> Capitalism is certainly flawed and is culpable , in part , for the global climate change that challenges us today . But capitalist innovation is already bringing about the solutions . Just watch . <p> You can comment on most stories on winnipegfreepress.com . You can also agree or disagree with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a Winnipeg Free Press print or e-edition subscriber to join the conversation and give your feedback . 
@@8563078 <p> Prime Minister Justin Trudeau insists he has always been " crystal clear " about pipelines . <p> Every Canadian government , he explains , has understood its obligation to get products to foreign markets -- products such as grain , minerals , lumber and , yes , energy . <p> But , the Prime Minister argues , in today 's world , pipelines ( and presumably other large projects ) just ca n't be approved by regulatory bodies and then approved automatically by cabinet . Projects need acceptance by communities . They need to be environmentally safe . They need buy-in from aboriginal people . <p> Call the Prime Minister 's line of thinking a bet . It consists of believing that more discussion , more " inclusion " of interested parties in review of projects , more time , more criteria considered -- all of this additional scrutiny will enhance , not obstruct , pipelines ( and other large projects ) into becoming socially acceptable so that the government can give them the green light . <p> Maybe the Prime Minister will be proven correct . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and environmentalists will persuade them , or many of them , of the need for this or that pipeline -- or mine , road , hydro transmission line , dam , or other large-scale energy-related project . <p> We ca n't know yet whether the Prime Minister 's bet will be won or lost . Thus far , the omens are not encouraging . Nothing suggests that opponents of developments are much impressed by this new approach of " inclusion " and additional consultation , because their objections to process were really arguments to cloak their deeper opposition to the projects per se . <p> The plethora of environmental groups dug in against any exploitation or transportation of fossil fuels remains as determined in their opposition as ever . A few of them have accepted that Alberta 's new climate-change policy and the federal government 's new interest in climate change leaves them somewhat more open for discussion . But the environmental groups remain hostile to any pipeline project and many other natural-resource projects , too . <p> Ditto for some aboriginal groups . Groups favourable to projects get little media @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . But every pipeline project , and other major project , is accompanied by vocal aboriginal opponents whose attitudes are not likely to change with the Trudeau approach . <p> Those who want their communities to remain centred on hunting , fishing and gathering , as the Cree chief who signed the far-left Leap Manifesto recently explained , do n't want any commercial development , period . <p> As for communities , hostility in and around Vancouver to the twinning of the Kinder-Morgan pipeline to British Columbia 's Lower Mainland remains formidable . As does opposition from some communities in Quebec to the Energy East pipeline . <p> What remains completely vague about the Prime Minister 's " crystal clarity " is what level of support ( or opposition ) his government would require from environmentalists , aboriginals and communities . After all , what does " social licence " mean , a phrase used by opponents to projects ? Who defines it ? How does it get measured ? <p> Does achieving " social licence " mean the government must await the approval of opponents before a project can proceed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Energy Board that hold lengthy hearings and possess considerable technical expertise are really not that important because they do not reflect and can not evaluate " social licence " ? <p> Is the Prime Minister saying , at least implicitly , that at the end of any process , cabinet will decide based not on the regulators ' judgment but on the ministers ' sense of what 's politically acceptable ? That judgment , if you think about it , will be highly subjective , a trading off of factors pro and con , and therefore hardly something defined by " crystal " clarity . <p> Thus far , ministerial statements about injecting more environmental and aboriginal perspectives into decisions about pipelines have raised more questions than they have answered . Eventually , the government will have to make a decision about pipelines ( and other big projects ) and the criteria they will use remain today rather less than " crystal clear . " <p> Somebody is going to be disappointed , even outraged , regardless of what processes were used in judging projects . It 's been rather easy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the general subject of big projects without actually having had to make a decision . <p> Decisions will eventually have to be made -- at which point what is asserted to be " crystal clear , " but which manifestly is not , might be better understood .

" I was embarrassed to be receiving a leadership award from a President who thinks that leadership is not taking a stand against injustice and an institution that profits from climate change and remains complicit in human rights and environmental violations through its corporate investments , " she said . " Complicity is most definitely not leadership and it is our responsibility as students to not remain complicit in the violent decisions of this institution . Average life expectancies for the homeless have been estimated to be between 34 and 47 years old , while some studies have confirmed that homelessness cuts life expectancy by 50% . This has caused many , including those of us , who work in the streets with the homeless and vulnerably housed , to conclude that homelessness is a life-limiting disease or a terminal diagnosis . <p> How does this investigative piece of journalism relate to the movie Spotlight ? " <p> Let 's stop right there . <p> The UNFCCC , signed by former prime minister Brian Mulroney and other world leaders at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 , is the foundation upon which all UN climate agreements , including that reached in Paris and signed at the UN on April 22 , are based . <p> Article 4 of the UNFCCC states : <p> " The extent to which developing country Parties will effectively implement their commitments under the Convention will depend on the effective implementation by developed country Parties of their commitments under the Convention related to financial resources and transfer of technology and will take fully into account that economic and social development and poverty eradication are the first and overriding priorities of the developing country Parties . " <p> This means that , under treaties based on the UNFCCC , developing nations will keep their emission reduction commitments provided we pay them enough and give them enough of our technology . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ developing countries clearly may ignore their emission targets if they interfere with their " first and overriding priorities " of " economic and social development and poverty eradication .
